title: Working on remote machines with SSH
objective: By the end of this lesson you can log into a remote machine with a key instead of a password, copy files safely in both directions, and explain why the host key warning is the one prompt you must never click through.

blocks.text: Almost every Linux machine you will work on professionally is somewhere else. SSH is how you reach it: an encrypted session that gives you the same shell you have been using for this entire course, on a machine you may never physically see.

blocks.caption: The basics
lines: ssh server 'df -h /'                  # run one command and come straight back

blocks.text: A key pair is two matching files: a private key that never leaves your machine, and a public key you copy to every server you want to reach. The server challenges you, your machine answers using the private key, and nothing secret crosses the network — which is the whole point.

blocks.caption: Set it up once
lines: ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "laptop-2026"     # create a pair; set a passphrase when asked
ssh-copy-id songpon@server                 # install the PUBLIC key on the server
ssh songpon@server                         # no password prompt now
#  id_ed25519       <- private. never copy this anywhere. must be 600
#  id_ed25519.pub   <- public. safe to hand out

blocks.title: The private key is the credential
blocks.text: Anyone who copies that file becomes you on every server that trusts it. Give it a passphrase, keep its permissions at 600 — SSH refuses to use a key that is readable by others — and never paste it into a chat, a ticket, or a repository. Keys leaked into public repositories are a routine cause of real breaches.

items: Nothing reusable crosses the network, so a captured session reveals no secret to replay
There is nothing to guess — automated password-guessing against your server simply stops working
Access is removed per person by deleting one line on the server, without changing anything for anyone else
A passphrase means a stolen laptop is not immediately a stolen server

blocks.caption: scp for one file, rsync for everything else
lines: rsync -av ~/site/ web1:/var/www/site/  # copy only what changed
rsync -av --dry-run ~/site/ web1:/var/www/site/   # show what WOULD change first

blocks.title: rsync --dry-run is the habit from the safety lesson, applied remotely
blocks.text: A trailing slash on the source means 'the contents of this directory'; without it you copy the directory itself into the target, one level deeper than you meant. Run it with --dry-run first and read the list. This is the same look-then-act rule you learned for rm, and it matters more here because the mistake lands on another machine.
The warning you must never click through

blocks.caption: What a changed host key looks like
lines: @  WARNING: REMOTE HOST IDENTIFICATION HAS CHANGED!  @
IT IS POSSIBLE THAT SOMEONE IS DOING SOMETHING NASTY!

blocks.text: The first time you connect, SSH records the server's identity in ~/.ssh/known_hosts. If that identity later changes, either the server was genuinely rebuilt, or something is sitting between you and it, decrypting everything you type. Do not delete the known_hosts entry to make the message go away. Confirm with whoever runs the server that it was rebuilt, then remove the entry deliberately.

blocks.caption: In /etc/ssh/sshd_config
lines: PermitRootLogin no             # log in as yourself, then sudo
# keep your current session open until you have tested a NEW one

blocks.title: Test in a second window before you close the first
blocks.text: If the change is wrong, the session you already have is the only way back in. Open a new terminal, confirm you can still log in, and only then close the original. Locking yourself out of a remote server is a specific and very memorable way to learn this.

blocks.title: Set up key access end to end
steps: Run: ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "$(whoami)-$(hostname)"   (accept the default path, set a passphrase)
Run: ls -l ~/.ssh/                                       (note that the private key is 600)
Run: cat ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub                           (this is the half you may share)
If you have a server: ssh-copy-id user@server then ssh user@server
If you do not: ssh-copy-id "$(whoami)@localhost" then ssh "$(whoami)@localhost"
Add a Host block to ~/.ssh/config and connect using the short name
Run: rsync -av --dry-run ~/scripts/ /tmp/scripts-copy/    (see what would be copied)
blocks.expected: A key pair with correct permissions, a login that never asks for a password, a short alias that replaces a long command, and a dry-run listing of a copy you have not performed yet.

blocks.text: Look at what you can now do. You can explain what an operating system is actually doing. You can move around a filesystem, read and set permissions, and see what is running as whom. You can interrogate a log with a pipeline, reshape text with sed and awk, write a script that fails safely, schedule it to run unattended, and reach another machine securely to do all of it there.

blocks.title: What to build next
blocks.text: The habit that carries you further than any single command: when a machine confuses you, ask the machine. A man page, a file in /etc, a log in /var/log, a process list, a crontab. Everything after this course — networking, hardening, incident response, cloud — is built on exactly what you just learned, and assumes you can find these answers yourself.

cheatsheet: ssh user@host · ssh -p PORT · ssh host 'command' runs one command remotely
ssh-keygen -t ed25519 creates a key pair · ssh-copy-id installs the public half
Private key never leaves your machine and must be mode 600
Keys beat passwords: nothing reusable crosses the network and nothing can be guessed
~/.ssh/config turns a long command into a short host alias
scp for a single file · rsync -av for trees · always --dry-run first
A trailing slash on an rsync source means 'the contents of', not the directory itself
A changed host key means rebuilt server OR interception — verify, never just delete the entry
PasswordAuthentication no and PermitRootLogin no, tested in a second session before closing the first

checkpoint.prompt: Which file may you safely copy to a server?

choices.D: Both keys, so the server can verify them

checkpoint.explanation: Only the public half is meant to be distributed. The private key is the credential itself and never leaves your machine.

checkpoint.prompt: Why is key-based authentication considered stronger than a password?

choices.A: Keys are shorter and easier to type
choices.B: Nothing reusable is sent across the network and there is nothing for an automated attack to guess

checkpoint.explanation: The private key answers a challenge without being transmitted. Password guessing against the service simply has nothing to work with.

checkpoint.prompt: SSH warns that the remote host identification has changed. What do you do?

choices.A: Delete the known_hosts entry so the warning stops
choices.B: Stop and confirm with whoever runs the server whether it was rebuilt — the alternative explanation is that something is intercepting the connection

checkpoint.explanation: Only two things produce that message: a legitimately rebuilt server, or an interception. Clearing the entry to silence it removes the only warning you would get for the second case.

checkpoint.prompt: You are about to disable password authentication on a remote server. What is the safe procedure?

choices.A: Apply the change, close the session, and reconnect
choices.B: Apply the change, then test a NEW session in a second window while keeping the current one open
choices.C: Reboot the server after changing the config
choices.D: Change it only from the physical console

checkpoint.explanation: The open session is your way back in if the new configuration is wrong. Verify a fresh login works before you give that up.

checkpoint.prompt: What does the trailing slash change in rsync -av ~/site/ web1:/var/www/site/ ?

choices.B: It copies the contents of ~/site into the target; without it, the site directory itself is placed inside the target
choices.D: It deletes files at the destination

checkpoint.explanation: This one character decides whether you get /var/www/site/index.html or /var/www/site/site/index.html — which is exactly why --dry-run comes first.
